questions.question: A compound Poisson loss has $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)$ and every severity equals $2$, so $S=2N$. Why is $S$ not an ordinary Poisson variable?
options: Its expected total is twice the frequency mean.
Its positive support omits every odd integer.
Its claim count includes a probability of zero.
Its severities are constant rather than random.

questions.question: A compound Poisson loss has intensity $\lambda>0$ and independent iid strictly positive continuous severities. Can its total distribution be fully continuous?
options: Yes; continuous summands eliminate all point masses.
Yes; a positive count is certain at positive intensity.
No; every positive total value must also be an atom.
No; it has mass $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$ at zero.

questions.question: In a compound Poisson model, $N$ has intensity $\lambda$, and iid severities independently fall in disjoint exhaustive categories with probabilities $p_1,\ldots,p_k$. Which description of category counts before conditioning on $N$ is valid for every such intensity and category scheme?
options: Independent Poisson counts each of mean $\lambda$.
Independent Poisson counts of means $\lambda p_j$.
Dependent counts because they sum to the total.
Fixed counts equal to $\lambda p_j$.

questions.question: A compound Poisson total uses intensity $4$ and independent iid severities with mean $3$. What is its expected total loss?
A compound Poisson total has intensity $2$. Independent iid severities have mean $3$ and variance $4$. What is its aggregate variance?
A compound Poisson loss has intensity $2$ and fixed severity $3$, so $S=3N$ with $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(2)$. What is $\mathbb{P}(S=6)$?
A compound Poisson loss has intensity $1/2$. Each independent severity is 1 or 2 with equal probabilities. For the natural-log argument $t=\log2$, what is $M_S(t)=\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tS}]$?
options: $\mathrm{e}^2$.

questions.question: A compound Poisson loss has intensity $\lambda>0$ and non-negative iid severities independent of count. At a real argument $t$, the severity exponential moment $\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{e}^{tX}]$ is infinite. Can the aggregate exponential moment still be finite?
options: Yes; Poisson counts have finite exponential moments.
Yes; sufficiently small positive intensity makes it finite.
No; the aggregate count must also have infinite mean.
No; the one-claim event already contributes infinity.

questions.question: A compound Poisson loss has intensity $\lambda>0$. An independent severity is zero with probability $p_0\in(0,1)$ and otherwise strictly positive. Which formula gives the zero-total probability for every such intensity and zero-severity probability?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda(1-p_0)}$.
$\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$.
$\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda p_0}$.
$p_0\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda}$.

questions.question: A compound Poisson model permits intensity $\lambda=0$. Its iid severities are non-negative and finite almost surely but have infinite second moment. What can be concluded about aggregate variance at this boundary?
options: It is infinite because the severity second moment is infinite.
It is undefined because the raw-moment formula gives an indeterminate product.
It is zero because no severity is ever included.
It is positive because unused severities are still random.

questions.question: A compound Poisson model has intensity $6$. Each claim independently falls in category A with probability $1/6$, category B with probability $1/3$, or a remaining category. What is the probability that both A and B have zero claims?
options: $\mathrm{e}^{-1}+\mathrm{e}^{-2}$.

questions.question: Two compound Poisson losses both have intensity 1. Model A severities are 0 or 2 with equal probabilities; model B severities are 0, 1, 3 with probabilities $1/3,1/2,1/6$. Severities satisfy the usual iid/count-independence assumptions. Both severity laws have mean 1 and second moment 2. Must the aggregate laws coincide?
options: Yes; mean and variance determine every aggregate law.
No; their zero-total probabilities differ.
Yes; matching intensity fixes the severity contribution.
No; their aggregate variances already differ.

questions.question: Let $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)$ be independent of a common amount $Z$, which is 0 or 2 with equal probabilities. Every claim uses $X_i=Z$, and $S=NZ$. Its aggregate mean is 1, agreeing with intensity times mean severity. Does this mean agreement establish the usual compound Poisson model?
options: Yes; each severity has the same two-point law.
Yes; independence of count guarantees independent severities.
No; the severities share randomness and are not iid.
No; the count is dependent on the common amount.

questions.question: An analyst proposes a compound Poisson model with unknown positive intensity and independent iid severities constrained to $1\le X\le3$. The target aggregate mean is 10 and variance is 50. Is this moment target feasible?
options: Yes; increasing intensity alone achieves variance 50.
Yes; variance may be five times mean within this range.
No; aggregate variance must equal aggregate mean.
No; aggregate variance cannot exceed 30 at mean 10.

questions.question: A compound Poisson model has unknown intensity $\lambda>0$. Each independent severity is 1 with probability $1-p$ and 2 with probability $p\in[0,1]$. Aggregate mean and variance are 6 and 10. Which pair $(\lambda,p)$ is forced by these moments?

Model A has Poisson claim intensity $1$ and every severity equals $1$. Model B has Poisson claim intensity $2$ and iid severities equal to $0$ or $1$ with equal probabilities, independent of the count. What can be concluded about the two aggregate loss laws?
options: They differ: model B has twice the mean loss of model A.
They coincide: both aggregate losses are $\operatorname{Pois}(1)$.
They differ: model B has zero-total probability $\mathrm{e}^{-2}$.
They coincide because both claim counts have mean $1$.
